title: Type drift between Parquet and CSV
prompt: Before moving a feed from Parquet to CSV, the team wants to see which column types would drift. Write `solve(trips)` so it saves the trips both ways and reports, for every column, the type each copy comes back with.
rules: Save all of `trips` as Parquet at `parquet_path` and as CSV with a header at `csv_path`, replacing earlier copies.
Read the Parquet copy back as it is, and the CSV copy with its header and `inferSchema=True`, the way a tool that guesses types would.
Return `column_name`, `parquet_type` and `csv_type`, all text, one row per column of `trips`, in any order. Types are written as `dtypes` shows them, such as `decimal(8,2)` or `double`.
Columns are matched by name; every column of `trips` appears once.
hints: `df.dtypes` lists `(name, type)` pairs; `dict(df.dtypes)` makes them easy to look up by name.
Build a list of `(name, parquet_type, csv_type)` tuples with a Python loop over the columns.
`spark.createDataFrame(rows, "column_name STRING, parquet_type STRING, csv_type STRING")` turns the list into the result.
starter:
def solve(trips):
    parquet_path = "/tmp/taxi/drift_parquet"
    csv_path = "/tmp/taxi/drift_csv"
    # Save trips both ways, read both back and return one row per column.
    return trips
explanation: Write both copies, read both back, and compare their `dtypes`: `p = dict(spark.read.parquet(parquet_path).dtypes)` and `c = dict(spark.read.csv(csv_path, header=True, inferSchema=True).dtypes)`, then `spark.createDataFrame([(name, p[name], c[name]) for name in trips.columns], "column_name STRING, parquet_type STRING, csv_type STRING")`. Parquet gives back the original types. The guessed CSV types drift: every money column becomes `double`, timestamps are recognised again, and a column with no values at all, or every column of an empty file, comes back as `string`, because there's nothing to guess from.
